I. Introduction¶

The ability to accurately forecast liquidity within portfolios is a core pillar of modern risk management and regulatory compliance. High-frequency liquidity prediction models empower asset managers to optimize cash allocation, reduce costly drawdowns, and maintain operational flexibility—directly contributing to enhanced fund performance and client confidence. Moreover, the development of robust, explainable models enables more transparent portfolio oversight, more reliable stress-testing, and clearer communication of liquidity risk.

The methodologies and results presented in this project are designed to anticipate potential liquidity trends by combining advanced machine learning with interpretable analytics. Due to the proprietary nature and confidentiality constraints surrounding individual fund-level data, the subsequent academic analysis focuses on aggregated model performance and explainability. Results are examined in detail through synthetic portfolios grouped by major asset classes—namely equities, fixed income, and multi-asset funds. This aggregation ensures that all technical findings can be scrutinized, benchmarked, and interpreted without compromising sensitive commercial information.

Technical Methodology¶

The empirical investigation centers on the liquidity dynamics of portfolios regulated under the UCITS (Undertakings for Collective Investment in Transferable Securities) framework—a set of European Union directives that set rigorous standards for liquidity, diversification, and investor protection. UCITS portfolios typically encompass a diversified set of assets across geographies and sectors, and are subject to daily liquidity and transparency requirements.

The modeling pipeline employs a comprehensive, multi-model approach:

  • Univariate time series model (ARIMA) provide statistical baselines and capture autoregressive liquidity patterns.
  • Machine learning techniques (Random Forest, XGBoost) leverage extended feature sets, including lagged risk and performance indicators, rolling portfolio exposures, and market-based signals.
  • Feature engineering integrates domain-relevant variables such as present and lagged liquidity, portfolio value, value at risk (VaR), conditional VaR (CVaR), transaction costs, and commitment exposures, with rolling statistics and exponential moving averages.
  • Model explainability is prioritized through the use of SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values, enabling the identification and aggregation of the most influential drivers of liquidity risk at both fund and asset class levels.
  • Distillation of complex model behavior into simpler, more interpretable regressions based on features importance and benchmarking.

Models are evaluated through rigorous out-of-sample rolling validation, with performance metrics including mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), and R². Aggregation at the asset class level not only protects confidentiality but also enables the analysis of systemic liquidity risk factors and the robustness of model insights across different segments of the fund universe.

Description of Portfolio Liquidity and Risk Variables¶

Variable Description
DCLG_ID Unique portfolio identifier
FUND_NAME Name of the fund or portfolio
ACLASS Asset class category (e.g., Equity, Fixed Income, Multi Asset)
DATE_C Calendar date of the observation
Liquidity Profile CASH Immediate cash available in the portfolio
Liquidity Profile incl. SD [Ptf] 1M Portfolio liquidity: proportion of assets that can be liquidated within 1 month
Liquidity Profile incl. SD [Ptf] 1Q Portfolio liquidity: proportion of assets that can be liquidated within (3 months)
Liquidity Profile incl. SD [Ptf] 1S Portfolio liquidity: proportion of assets that can be liquidated within 1 semester (6 months)
Liquidity Profile incl. SD [Ptf] 1Y Portfolio liquidity: proportion of assets that can be liquidated within 1 year
Liquidity Profile incl. SD [Ptf] 1W Portfolio liquidity: proportion of assets that can be liquidated within within 1 week
Liquidity Profile incl. SD [Ptf] 10 Portfolio liquidity: proportion of assets that can be liquidated within 10 days
Ptf PV Portfolio present value (market value)
SR acc Subscription/Redemption accumulated (net investor flows over period)
TCOST_CUS30_WATE_TD_1D Transaction cost estimate (30-day custom window, weighted, 1-day horizon)
TCOST_TOTAL_WATE_TD_1D Total transaction cost estimate (all-in, 1-day horizon)
UCITS - Commitment UCITS regulatory leverage commitment calculation
VaR 99% 1Y PTF Value at Risk (99% confidence, 1 year horizon, portfolio)
VaR 99% 1Y REF Value at Risk (99% confidence, 1 year horizon, reference index)
cVaR 99% 1Y PTF Conditional Value at Risk (expected shortfall, 99% confidence, 1 year horizon, portfolio)
cVaR 99% 1Y REF Conditional Value at Risk (expected shortfall, 99% confidence, 1 year horizon, reference index)

In [9]:
# Initialize a dictionary to store cleaned data
cleaned_data = {}

# Get unique DCLG_ID values from merged
unique_funds = merged['DCLG_ID'].unique()

# Define liquidity-related columns
liquidity_cols = [
    'Liquidity Profile CASH',
    'Liquidity Profile incl. SD [Ptf] 1M',
    'Liquidity Profile incl. SD [Ptf] 1Q',
    'Liquidity Profile incl. SD [Ptf] 1S',
    'Liquidity Profile incl. SD [Ptf] 1W',
    'Liquidity Profile incl. SD [Ptf] 1Y',
    'Liquidity Profile incl. SD [Ptf] >1Y'
]

# Tolerance level around 1.0
tolerance = 0.001

# Loop through each fund
for fund in unique_funds:
    fund_df = merged[merged['DCLG_ID'] == fund].copy()

    # Drop duplicates
    fund_df.drop_duplicates(inplace=True)

    # Replace 0s and outliers with NaN
    for col in liquidity_cols:
        threshold = fund_df[col].quantile(0.99)
        mask = (fund_df[col] == 0) | (fund_df[col] > threshold)
        fund_df.loc[mask, col] = np.nan

    # Fill missing with the mean of the next 7 values (including the current one)
    fund_df[liquidity_cols] = fund_df[liquidity_cols].fillna(
        fund_df[liquidity_cols].shift(-1).rolling(window=7, min_periods=1).mean()
)

    # Recalculate liquidity sum
    fund_df['liquidity_sum'] = fund_df[liquidity_cols].sum(axis=1)

    # Normalize rows where liquidity sum ≠ 1 (within tolerance)
    def normalize_row(row):
        if abs(row['liquidity_sum'] - 1) > tolerance:
            nonzero_cols = [col for col in liquidity_cols if row[col] > 0]
            total = row[nonzero_cols].sum()
            if total > 0:
                for col in nonzero_cols:
                    row[col] = row[col] / total
                row['liquidity_sum'] = 1.0
        return row

    fund_df = fund_df.apply(normalize_row, axis=1)

    # Save to dictionary
    cleaned_data[fund] = fund_df

III. Modeling_Building¶

ARIMA (Autoregressive integrated moving average), Random Forest & XGBoost¶

This chapter outlines a series of utility functions and a comprehensive modeling approach for forecasting fund performance using time series data. The key components include:

1. Utility Functions¶

  • build_fund_name_map: Creates a mapping of fund names to their respective IDs from cleaned data.
  • calculate_metrics: Computes various performance metrics (e.g., MAE, RMSE, R²) to evaluate model predictions against actual values.
  • extended_lag_features:
    • Generates lagged features, differences, and rolling statistics for specified columns in the dataset to enhance predictive modeling.
    • For each specified column, it creates:
      • Lagged values for specified time lags (0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 14 days).
      • Differences between current and lagged values.
      • A 7-day rolling mean.
      • A 7-day rolling standard deviation.
      • A 7-day exponential moving average (EMA).
  • impute_with_special_forward_rolling_mean: Handles missing values by applying a forward rolling mean strategy.
  • sanitize_feature_names: Cleans feature names for better readability.
  • make_business_friendly_name: Converts technical feature names into more understandable business-friendly formats.

2. Main Results Structure¶

  • Initializes a results dictionary to store metrics and curves for different forecasting models (ARIMA, Random Forest, and XGBoost).

3. Fund-Level Rolling Forecast Modeling¶

  • The process_fund function implements a rolling forecast strategy for each fund, utilizing ARIMA for time series forecasting and Random Forest and XGBoost for regression tasks.
  • The function processes the data by filtering for relevant columns, creating features, and splitting the data into training and testing sets.
  • It performs rolling predictions for each model, calculates metrics, and captures feature importances and SHAP values for interpretability.

4. Parallel Processing¶

  • The chapter concludes with a parallel execution of the process_fund function across multiple funds, aggregating results into the predefined structure for further analysis.

Overall, this chapter provides a robust framework for forecasting fund performance, leveraging advanced statistical and machine learning techniques to derive insights from financial data.

# ---------- Utility Functions ----------
def build_fund_name_map(cleaned_data):
   return {str(df["FUND_NAME"].iloc[0]) if "FUND_NAME" in df.columns else str(fid): fid
           for fid, df in cleaned_data.items()}
def calculate_metrics(y_true, y_pred):
   df = pd.DataFrame({'y_true': y_true, 'y_pred': y_pred}).dropna()
   if len(df) == 0:
       return {k: np.nan for k in ['MAE', 'RMSE', 'MAPE', 'Median_AE', 'R2', 'Bias', 'Explained_Var']}
   return {
       'MAE': mean_absolute_error(df['y_true'], df['y_pred']),
       'RMSE': np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(df['y_true'], df['y_pred'])),
       'MAPE': mean_absolute_percentage_error(df['y_true'], df['y_pred']),
       'Median_AE': median_absolute_error(df['y_true'], df['y_pred']),
       'R2': r2_score(df['y_true'], df['y_pred']),
       'Bias': np.mean(df['y_pred'] - df['y_true']),
       'Explained_Var': explained_variance_score(df['y_true'], df['y_pred']),
   }
def extended_lag_features(df, cols):
   for col in cols:
       for lag in [0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 14]:  
           df[f'{col}_lag_{lag}'] = df[col].shift(lag)
           df[f'{col}_diff_{lag}'] = df[col].diff(lag).shift(1)
       df[f'{col}_rolling_mean_7'] = df[col].rolling(7).mean()
       df[f'{col}_rolling_std_7'] = df[col].rolling(7).std()
       df[f'{col}_ema_7'] = df[col].ewm(span=7, adjust=False).mean()
   return df
def impute_with_special_forward_rolling_mean(df, window=7):
   for col in df.columns:
       if df[col].isna().all():
           df[col] = df[col].shift(-window).rolling(window=window, min_periods=1).mean()
       else:
           df[col] = df[col].fillna(df[col].rolling(window, min_periods=1).mean()).fillna(df[col].mean())
   return df
def sanitize_feature_names(cols):
   return [col.replace('[','_').replace(']','_').replace('<','_').replace('>','_') for col in cols]
# Business-friendly feature name mapping
def make_business_friendly_name(tech_name):
   import re
   if "_lag_" in tech_name:
       col, lag = tech_name.split("_lag_")
       lag = int(lag)
       if lag == 0:
           return f"Current {col.replace('_',' ')}"
       else:
           return f"{col.replace('_',' ')} {lag} Day{'s' if lag>1 else ''} Ago"
   elif "_diff_" in tech_name:
       col, lag = tech_name.split("_diff_")
       lag = int(lag)
       return f"Change in {col.replace('_',' ')} Since {lag} Day{'s' if lag>1 else ''} Ago"
   elif "rolling_mean_7" in tech_name:
       col = tech_name.replace("_rolling_mean_7", "")
       return f"7-Day Average {col.replace('_',' ')}"
   elif "rolling_std_7" in tech_name:
       col = tech_name.replace("_rolling_std_7", "")
       return f"7-Day Volatility in {col.replace('_',' ')}"
   elif "ema_7" in tech_name:
       col = tech_name.replace("_ema_7", "")
       return f"7-Day Trend in {col.replace('_',' ')}"
   else:
       return tech_name.replace('_',' ').title()

# ---------- Fund-Level Rolling Forecast Modeling Function ----------
def process_fund(fund_name, fund_id):
   df = cleaned_data[fund_id].copy()
   if "DATE_C" not in df or "Liquidity Profile CASH" not in df:
       print(f"Skipping {fund_name}: missing DATE_C or Liquidity Profile CASH")
       return None
   df["DATE_C"] = pd.to_datetime(df["DATE_C"], errors="coerce")
   df.set_index("DATE_C", inplace=True)
   ts = df["Liquidity Profile CASH"]["2024-01-01":"2024-12-31"].dropna()
   if len(ts) < 30:
       print(f"Skipping {fund_name}: not enough data points after filtering (found {len(ts)})")
       return None
   train, test = ts["2024-01-01":"2024-10-31"], ts["2024-11-01":"2024-12-31"]
   # --- ARIMA Rolling T+1 Only ---
   arima_curves = {"y_train": train, "y_test": test}
   arima_metrics = {}
   for h in [1]:
       preds_arima, arima_actuals = [], []
       rolling_train = train.copy()
       rolling_test_idx = test.index[h-1:]
       for i in range(len(rolling_test_idx)):
           try:
               model = ARIMA(rolling_train, order=(0,0,1)).fit()
               forecast = model.forecast(steps=h)
               preds_arima.append(forecast.values[-1])
               arima_actuals.append(test.iloc[i + h - 1])
               rolling_train = pd.concat([rolling_train, pd.Series(test.iloc[i], index=[test.index[i]])])
           except Exception:
               preds_arima.append(np.nan)
               arima_actuals.append(np.nan)
       arima_curves[f"forecast_T+{h}"] = pd.Series(preds_arima, index=rolling_test_idx)
       arima_metrics[f"T+{h}"] = calculate_metrics(pd.Series(arima_actuals, index=rolling_test_idx), arima_curves[f"forecast_T+{h}"])
  
   # --- Feature Engineering ---
   all_features_raw = [col for col in df.columns if any(
       k in col for k in [
           "Liquidity Profile", "PV", "EU", "US", "SR acc", "VAR", "CVAR", "TCOST_", "UCITS - Commitment"
       ]
   )]
   df_feat = extended_lag_features(df[all_features_raw], all_features_raw)
   df_feat = impute_with_special_forward_rolling_mean(df_feat)
   df_feat["target"] = ts.shift(-1)
   df_feat.columns = sanitize_feature_names(df_feat.columns)
   features = [col for col in df_feat.columns if ('lag' in col or 'diff' in col or 'rolling' in col or 'ema' in col)]
   train_df, test_df = df_feat.loc[train.index], df_feat.loc[test.index]
   train_X, test_X = train_df[features], test_df[features]
   train_y, test_y = train_df["target"], test_df["target"]
   # --- Rolling T+1 for RF and XGB ---
   rf_curves = {"y_train": train_y, "y_test": test_y}
   xgb_curves = {"y_train": train_y, "y_test": test_y}
   rf_metrics, xgb_metrics = {}, {}
   rf_feature_importances, xgb_feature_importances = {}, {}
   rf_shap_values, xgb_shap_values = {}, {}
   rf_feature_names, xgb_feature_names = {}, {}
   for h in [1]:
       preds_rf, preds_xgb, actuals = [], [], []
       rf_importances_h, xgb_importances_h = [], []
       rolling_X_train = train_X.copy()
       rolling_y_train = train_y.copy()
       test_indices = test_X.index[h-1:]
       for i in range(len(test_indices)):
           X_pred = test_X.iloc[[i]]
           y_pred = test_y.iloc[i + h - 1]
           # Fit RF
           rf_model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=50, max_depth=7, random_state=42)
           rf_model.fit(rolling_X_train, rolling_y_train)
           rf_forecast = rf_model.predict(X_pred)[0]
           preds_rf.append(rf_forecast)
           rf_importances_h.append(pd.Series(rf_model.feature_importances_, index=features))
           # Fit XGB
           xgb_model = XGBRegressor(n_estimators=50, max_depth=7, tree_method='hist', random_state=42)
           rolling_X_train_xgb = rolling_X_train.copy()
           X_pred_xgb = X_pred.copy()
           rolling_X_train_xgb.columns = sanitize_feature_names(rolling_X_train_xgb.columns)
           X_pred_xgb.columns = sanitize_feature_names(X_pred_xgb.columns)
           xgb_model.fit(rolling_X_train_xgb, rolling_y_train)
           xgb_forecast = xgb_model.predict(X_pred_xgb)[0]
           preds_xgb.append(xgb_forecast)
           xgb_importances_h.append(pd.Series(xgb_model.feature_importances_, index=features))
           actuals.append(y_pred)
           if i + h - 1 < len(test_y):
               rolling_X_train = pd.concat([rolling_X_train, test_X.iloc[[i]]], axis=0)
               rolling_y_train = pd.concat([rolling_y_train, pd.Series(test_y.iloc[i], index=[test_X.index[i]])], axis=0)
       rf_curves[f"forecast_T+{h}"] = pd.Series(preds_rf, index=test_indices)
       xgb_curves[f"forecast_T+{h}"] = pd.Series(preds_xgb, index=test_indices)
       rf_metrics[f"T+{h}"] = calculate_metrics(pd.Series(actuals, index=test_indices), rf_curves[f"forecast_T+{h}"])
       xgb_metrics[f"T+{h}"] = calculate_metrics(pd.Series(actuals, index=test_indices), xgb_curves[f"forecast_T+{h}"])
       rf_feature_importances[f"T+{h}"] = pd.concat(rf_importances_h, axis=1).mean(axis=1).sort_values(ascending=False)
       xgb_feature_importances[f"T+{h}"] = pd.concat(xgb_importances_h, axis=1).mean(axis=1).sort_values(ascending=False)
       rf_feature_names[f"T+{h}"] = features
       xgb_feature_names[f"T+{h}"] = features
       # SHAP on first 10 predictions for speed
       try:
           explainer_rf = shap.TreeExplainer(rf_model)
           rf_shap_values[f"T+{h}"] = explainer_rf.shap_values(test_X[:10])
       except Exception as e:
           rf_shap_values[f"T+{h}"] = None
       try:
           explainer_xgb = shap.TreeExplainer(xgb_model)
           xgb_shap_values[f"T+{h}"] = explainer_xgb.shap_values(test_X[:10])
       except Exception as e:
           xgb_shap_values[f"T+{h}"] = None
   return (
       fund_name,
       arima_curves, arima_metrics,
       rf_curves, rf_metrics, rf_feature_importances, rf_shap_values, rf_feature_names,
       xgb_curves, xgb_metrics, xgb_feature_importances, xgb_shap_values, xgb_feature_names
   )
# ---------- Run Parallel Rolling Modeling & Populate Results Structure ----------
fund_name_map = build_fund_name_map(cleaned_data)
processed_results = Parallel(n_jobs=4)(
   delayed(process_fund)(name, fund_name_map[name]) for name in fund_name_map.keys()
)
for res in processed_results:
   if res:
       (fund_name,
        arima_curves, arima_metrics,
        rf_curves, rf_metrics, rf_feature_importances, rf_shap_values, rf_features,
        xgb_curves, xgb_metrics, xgb_feature_importances, xgb_shap_values, xgb_features) = res
       results['arima']['curves'][fund_name] = arima_curves
       results['arima']['metrics'][fund_name] = arima_metrics
       results['rf']['curves'][fund_name] = rf_curves
       results['rf']['metrics'][fund_name] = rf_metrics
       results['rf']['feature_importances'][fund_name] = rf_feature_importances
       results['rf']['shap_values'][fund_name] = rf_shap_values
       results['rf']['feature_names'][fund_name] = rf_features
       results['xgb']['curves'][fund_name] = xgb_curves
       results['xgb']['metrics'][fund_name] = xgb_metrics
       results['xgb']['feature_importances'][fund_name] = xgb_feature_importances
       results['xgb']['shap_values'][fund_name] = xgb_shap_values
       results['xgb']['feature_names'][fund_name] = xgb_features

# ---- Load the required data for further analysis ----
steps_ahead = 1  
# Asset class mapping and analysis fund list
asset_class_map = dict(zip(merged['FUND_NAME'], merged['ACLASS']))
all_asset_classes = ['All'] + sorted(set(asset_class_map.values()))
arima_funds = set(results['arima']['metrics'].keys())
rf_funds = set(results['rf']['metrics'].keys())
xgb_funds = set(results['xgb']['metrics'].keys())
fund_names = list(arima_funds & rf_funds & xgb_funds)

IV. Evaluation¶

In this analysis, we evaluate the performance of various forecasting models, specifically ARIMA, Random Forest, and XGBoost, using several metrics including Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), Median Absolute Error, R² (Explained Variance), and Bias.

To ensure the robustness of our findings, portfolios where the R² values for either Random Forest or XGBoost are lower than -0.5 are excluded from the analysis. This threshold helps to filter out models that do not provide meaningful predictions, thereby enhancing the overall quality of the results.

Feature Importance and SHAP Analysis¶

Feature importance is a critical aspect of model evaluation, as it helps to identify which variables have the most significant impact on the predictions. In this analysis, we utilize SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values to interpret the contributions of each feature to the model's predictions. SHAP values provide insights into how much each feature contributes to the difference between the model's prediction and the expected outcome.

The analysis includes:

  • Aggregated Feature Importance: We compute the average importance of features across different asset classes and models, allowing us to identify which features are consistently influential.
  • SHAP Value Analysis: We visualize the SHAP values for the top features, providing a clear understanding of their impact on the model's predictions. This visualization helps in interpreting the model's behavior and understanding the underlying data relationships.

By focusing on feature importance and SHAP values, we can derive actionable insights that inform decision-making and enhance the predictive capabilities of our models.

def style_best_values(tbl):
   style_df = pd.DataFrame('color: {}; font-weight: normal; font-size: 1em'.format(amundi_dark_blue),
                           index=tbl.index, columns=tbl.columns)
   for col in tbl.columns:
       if col in higher_is_better:
           best = tbl[col].idxmax()
       elif col == bias_col:
           best = (tbl[col].abs()).idxmin()
       else:
           best = tbl[col].idxmin()
       style_df.loc[best, col] = (
           'color: {}; font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.08em; text-decoration: underline'
           .format(amundi_dark_blue)
       )
   return style_df

               pred.append(np.average(vals, weights=weights))
           else:

       return np.array(pred)

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import shap
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as ticker
from IPython.display import display, HTML
import ipywidgets as widgets
N = 10  # Top features
def get_friendly(feat):
   if 'make_business_friendly_name' in globals():
       return make_business_friendly_name(feat)
   return feat
def wrap_feature_name(name, maxlen=18):
   """Wrap long feature names to two lines for SHAP plots."""
   name = str(name)
   if len(name) <= maxlen:
       return name
   if ' ' in name[:maxlen]:
       idx = name.rfind(' ', 0, maxlen)
       return name[:idx] + '\n' + name[idx+1:]
   else:
       return name[:maxlen] + '\n' + name[maxlen:]
def aggregate_feature_importance(model_key):
   feat_rows = []
   for fund in filtered_funds:
       asset_class = asset_class_map.get(fund, 'Unknown')
       fi_dict = results[model_key]['feature_importances'][fund]['T+1']
       for feat, val in fi_dict.items():
           feat_rows.append({'Asset Class': asset_class, 'Feature': feat, 'Importance': val})
   df_fi = pd.DataFrame(feat_rows)
   agg_fi = df_fi.groupby(['Asset Class', 'Feature'])['Importance'].mean().reset_index()
   return agg_fi
def aggregate_shap_for_asset_class(model_key, asset_class_code):
   shap_values_all = []
   features_all = []
   for fund in filtered_funds:
       if asset_class_map.get(fund, None) != asset_class_code:
           continue
       shap_vals = results[model_key]['shap_values'][fund]['T+1']
       feat_names = results[model_key]['feature_names'][fund]['T+1']
       if shap_vals is not None and feat_names is not None:
           shap_values_all.append(shap_vals)
           features_all.append(pd.DataFrame(columns=feat_names, data=shap_vals).iloc[:, :])
   if not shap_values_all or not features_all:
       return None, None
   shap_all = np.vstack(shap_values_all)
   feature_all_names = features_all[0].columns
   mean_abs = np.abs(shap_all).mean(axis=0)
   top_idx = np.argsort(mean_abs)[::-1][:N]
   shap_top = shap_all[:, top_idx]
   feature_names_top = [feature_all_names[i] for i in top_idx]
   return shap_top, feature_names_top
# Table style with alternate row coloring
table_style = [
   {'selector': 'tbody tr:nth-child(even)', 'props': [('background-color', '#F6F6F6')]},
   {'selector': 'th', 'props': [('background-color', '#eeeeee'), ('font-size', '1.03em')]}
]
# --- Aggregate importances ---
agg_rf = aggregate_feature_importance('rf')
agg_xgb = aggregate_feature_importance('xgb')
agg_ensemble = pd.merge(
   agg_rf, agg_xgb,
   on=['Asset Class', 'Feature'],
   how='outer',
   suffixes=('_rf', '_xgb')
)
agg_ensemble[['Importance_rf', 'Importance_xgb']] = agg_ensemble[['Importance_rf', 'Importance_xgb']].fillna(0)
agg_ensemble['Ensemble Avg Importance'] = agg_ensemble[['Importance_rf', 'Importance_xgb']].mean(axis=1)
agg_ensemble['Feature Name'] = agg_ensemble['Feature'].map(get_friendly)
for aclass in sorted(set(agg_ensemble['Asset Class'])):
   full_name = asset_class_full.get(aclass, aclass)
   top_ens = agg_ensemble[agg_ensemble['Asset Class'] == aclass].sort_values(
       'Ensemble Avg Importance', ascending=False
   ).head(N)

       }
   ).reset_index(drop=True)
   ens_html = ens_tbl.style.set_table_styles(table_style).set_properties(**{

   }).hide(axis="index").to_html()
   
   table_widget = widgets.HTML(

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import shap
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as ticker
from IPython.display import display, HTML
N = 10  # Top features
def get_friendly(feat):
   if 'make_business_friendly_name' in globals():
       return make_business_friendly_name(feat)
   return feat
def wrap_feature_name(name, maxlen=18):
   """Wrap long feature names to two lines for SHAP plots."""
   name = str(name)
   if len(name) <= maxlen:
       return name
   if ' ' in name[:maxlen]:
       idx = name.rfind(' ', 0, maxlen)
       return name[:idx] + '\n' + name[idx+1:]
   else:
       return name[:maxlen] + '\n' + name[maxlen:]
def aggregate_feature_importance(model_key):
   feat_rows = []
   for fund in filtered_funds:
       asset_class = asset_class_map.get(fund, 'Unknown')
       fi_dict = results[model_key]['feature_importances'][fund]['T+1']
       for feat, val in fi_dict.items():
           feat_rows.append({'Asset Class': asset_class, 'Feature': feat, 'Importance': val})
   df_fi = pd.DataFrame(feat_rows)
   agg_fi = df_fi.groupby(['Asset Class', 'Feature'])['Importance'].mean().reset_index()
   return agg_fi
def aggregate_shap_for_asset_class(model_key, asset_class_code):
   shap_values_all = []
   features_all = []
   for fund in filtered_funds:
       if asset_class_map.get(fund, None) != asset_class_code:
           continue
       shap_vals = results[model_key]['shap_values'][fund]['T+1']
       feat_names = results[model_key]['feature_names'][fund]['T+1']
       if shap_vals is not None and feat_names is not None:
           shap_values_all.append(shap_vals)
           features_all.append(pd.DataFrame(columns=feat_names, data=shap_vals).iloc[:, :])
   if not shap_values_all or not features_all:
       return None, None
   shap_all = np.vstack(shap_values_all)
   feature_all_names = features_all[0].columns
   mean_abs = np.abs(shap_all).mean(axis=0)
   top_idx = np.argsort(mean_abs)[::-1][:N]
   shap_top = shap_all[:, top_idx]
   feature_names_top = [feature_all_names[i] for i in top_idx]
   return shap_top, feature_names_top
# Table style with alternate row coloring
table_style = [
   {'selector': 'tbody tr:nth-child(even)', 'props': [('background-color', '#F6F6F6')]},
   {'selector': 'th', 'props': [('background-color', '#eeeeee'), ('font-size', '1.03em')]}
]
# --- Aggregate importances ---
agg_rf = aggregate_feature_importance('rf')
agg_xgb = aggregate_feature_importance('xgb')
agg_ensemble = pd.merge(
   agg_rf, agg_xgb,
   on=['Asset Class', 'Feature'],
   how='outer',
   suffixes=('_rf', '_xgb')
)
agg_ensemble[['Importance_rf', 'Importance_xgb']] = agg_ensemble[['Importance_rf', 'Importance_xgb']].fillna(0)
agg_ensemble['Ensemble Avg Importance'] = agg_ensemble[['Importance_rf', 'Importance_xgb']].mean(axis=1)
agg_ensemble['Feature Name'] = agg_ensemble['Feature'].map(get_friendly)
for aclass in sorted(set(agg_ensemble['Asset Class'])):
   full_name = asset_class_full.get(aclass, aclass)
   top_ens = agg_ensemble[agg_ensemble['Asset Class'] == aclass].sort_values(

V. Model_Distillation¶

In this section, we focus on the distillation of model predictions for cash liquidity forecasting using the top-performing features from Random Forest (RF), XGBoost (XGB), and an ensemble approach. The goal is to create simplified models that retain the predictive power of the original complex models while being easier to interpret and deploy.

Structure Initialization¶

We begin by ensuring that the necessary structures for storing the distillate results are created if they do not already exist. This includes separate entries for distillate models based on RF, XGB, and an ensemble of both.

Feature Selection¶

A helper function is defined to retrieve the top features for each model type. The distillation process involves iterating through each asset class and selecting the relevant features for the models. For each fund within the asset class, we prepare the data by:

  1. Data Preparation:

    • Extracting the time series data for the "Liquidity Profile CASH".
    • Creating lagged features and imputing missing values.
    • Defining the target variable for prediction.

  2. Model Training:

    • A linear regression model is trained on the cleaned training data.
    • Predictions are made on the test set, and the results are stored in the appropriate structure for later analysis.

Aggregated Predictions¶

After training the models, we aggregate the predictions for each asset class. This involves calculating weighted averages of the predictions based on the fund's present value (PV) to ensure that larger funds have a proportionally greater impact on the aggregated results.

Visualization¶

Finally, we visualize the distillate model predictions against the actual cash liquidity values for each asset class. The plots include:

  • Actual Values: Displayed for both training and testing periods.
  • Model Predictions: Shown for each distillate model, allowing for a clear comparison of performance.

This distillation process not only simplifies the models but also provides insights into the predictive capabilities of the selected features, enhancing interpretability and usability in real-world applications.

def get_distillate_features_dict(model_type):
   if model_type == 'distillate_rf':
       return top_rf_features
   elif model_type == 'distillate_xgb':
       return top_xgb_features
   elif model_type == 'distillate_ensemble':
       return top_ensemble_features
for model_type in ['distillate_rf', 'distillate_xgb', 'distillate_ensemble']:
   top_features_dict = get_distillate_features_dict(model_type)
   for asset_class in top_features_dict:
       features = top_features_dict[asset_class]
       funds_in_class = [f for f in filtered_funds if asset_class_map.get(f, None) == asset_class]
       for fund_name in funds_in_class:
           fund_id = build_fund_name_map(cleaned_data).get(fund_name, None)
           if fund_id is None or fund_id not in cleaned_data:
               continue
           df = cleaned_data[fund_id].copy()
           if "DATE_C" not in df or "Liquidity Profile CASH" not in df:
               continue
           df["DATE_C"] = pd.to_datetime(df["DATE_C"], errors="coerce")
           df.set_index("DATE_C", inplace=True)
           ts = df["Liquidity Profile CASH"]["2024-01-01":"2024-12-31"].dropna()
           if len(ts) < 30:
               continue
           train = ts["2024-01-01":"2024-10-31"]
           test = ts["2024-11-01":"2024-12-31"]
           all_features_raw = [col for col in df.columns if any(
               k in col for k in [
                   "Liquidity Profile", "PV", "EU", "US", "SR acc", "VAR", "CVAR", "TCOST_", "UCITS - Commitment"
               ]
           )]
           df_feat = extended_lag_features(df[all_features_raw], all_features_raw)
           df_feat = impute_with_special_forward_rolling_mean(df_feat)
           df_feat["target"] = ts.shift(-1)
           df_feat.columns = sanitize_feature_names(df_feat.columns)
           available_features = [f for f in features if f in df_feat.columns]
           train_df, test_df = df_feat.loc[train.index], df_feat.loc[test.index]
           train_X, test_X = train_df[available_features], test_df[available_features]
           train_y, test_y = train_df["target"], test_df["target"]
           train_mask = train_X.notnull().all(axis=1) & train_y.notnull()
           test_mask = test_X.notnull().all(axis=1) & test_y.notnull()
           train_X_clean, train_y_clean = train_X[train_mask], train_y[train_mask]
           test_X_clean, test_y_clean = test_X[test_mask], test_y[test_mask]
           if train_X_clean.shape[0] == 0 or test_X_clean.shape[0] == 0:
               continue
           model = LinearRegression()
           model.fit(train_X_clean, train_y_clean)
           preds = model.predict(test_X_clean)
           # Save in the expected results structure for plotting
           if fund_name not in results[model_type]['curves']:
               results[model_type]['curves'][fund_name] = {}
           results[model_type]['curves'][fund_name]['forecast_T+1'] = pd.Series(preds, index=test_X_clean.index)
           results[model_type]['curves'][fund_name]['y_test'] = test_y_clean  # optionally store actuals too

   'DISTILLATE_XGB': "Distillate (XGB)",

}
distillate_curves_dicts = {
   "DISTILLATE_RF": distillate_rf_curves,

for asset_code, full_name in asset_class_full.items():
   funds_in_class = [f for f in filtered_funds if asset_class_map.get(f, None) == asset_code]
   if not funds_in_class:
       print(f"No funds for asset class {full_name}")
       continue
   # Collect train/test dates as before
   train_dates = set()
   test_dates = set()
   for fund in funds_in_class:
       train_dates.update(results['rf']['curves'][fund]['y_train'].index)
       test_dates.update(results['rf']['curves'][fund]['y_test'].index)
   train_dates = np.array(sorted(train_dates))
   test_dates = np.array(sorted(test_dates))
   def weighted_avg(dates, which):
       y_agg = []
       for date in dates:
           vals = []
           weights = []
           for fund in funds_in_class:
               curve = results['rf']['curves'][fund][which]
               if date in curve.index:
                   val = curve.loc[date]
                   if np.isfinite(val):
                       vals.append(val)
                       weights.append(fund_pv_map.get(fund, 1.0))
           if weights and np.sum(weights) > 0:
               y_agg.append(np.average(vals, weights=weights))
           else:
               y_agg.append(np.nan)
       return np.array(y_agg)
   agg_actual_train = weighted_avg(train_dates, 'y_train')
   agg_actual_test = weighted_avg(test_dates, 'y_test')
   def agg_distillate_forecast(model_curves_dict):
       pred = []
       for date in test_dates:
           vals = []
           weights = []
           for fund in funds_in_class:
               if fund in model_curves_dict and 'forecast_T+1' in model_curves_dict[fund]:
                   series = model_curves_dict[fund]['forecast_T+1']
                   if date in series.index:
                       val = series.loc[date]
                       if np.isfinite(val):
                           vals.append(val)
                           weights.append(fund_pv_map.get(fund, 1.0))
           if weights and np.sum(weights) > 0:
               pred.append(np.average(vals, weights=weights))
           else:
               pred.append(np.nan)
       return np.array(pred)
   
   # --- PLOTTING ---
   fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(15, 6))
   # Training Actual (solid gray)
   ax.plot(train_dates, 100*agg_actual_train, color="#555555", lw=2.3, label="Actual (train)", zorder=1)
   # Test Actual (solid black)
   ax.plot(test_dates, 100*agg_actual_test, color="black", lw=2.7, label="Actual (test)", zorder=2)
   for model_key in ["DISTILLATE_RF", "DISTILLATE_XGB", "DISTILLATE_ENSEMBLE"]:
       if model_key in distillate_curves_dicts:
           agg_pred = agg_distillate_forecast(distillate_curves_dicts[model_key])
           linestyle = "--" if model_key == "DISTILLATE_RF" else "-." if model_key == "DISTILLATE_XGB" else ":"
           ax.plot(test_dates, 100*agg_pred, color=distillate_colors[model_key],
                   lw=2.3, linestyle=linestyle, label=distillate_labels[model_key])
   
   # Title, labels
   ax.set_title(f"{full_name}: Distillate Models vs Actual (Weighted, Test Period)", fontsize=16, color=amundi_dark_blue, fontweight='bold', pad=18)
   ax.set_xlabel("Date", fontsize=13)
   ax.set_ylabel("Cash Liquidity (%)", fontsize=13)
   ymin = min(np.nanmin(100*agg_actual_train), np.nanmin(100*agg_actual_test)) * 0.95
   ymax = max(np.nanmax(100*agg_actual_train), np.nanmax(100*agg_actual_test)) * 1.05
   ax.set_ylim(ymin, ymax)
   ax.legend(loc='center left', bbox_to_anchor=(1, 0.5), frameon=True, fontsize=12, title_fontsize=13)
   ax.grid(alpha=0.18)
   plt.tight_layout()
   plt.show()

pretty_order = [model_pretty[m] for m in model_display_order]
higher_is_better = ["R² (Explained Variance)"]
bias_col = "Bias"
# ---- Combine all rows (original + distillate, as previously built) ----
all_rows = rows + distillate_rows_rf + distillate_rows_xgb + distillate_rows_ens
df = pd.DataFrame(all_rows)
def weighted_mean(group, value_col):
   d = group[value_col]
   w = group['Weight']
   try:
       return np.average(d, weights=w)
   except ZeroDivisionError:
       return np.nan
agg_rows = []
for (aclass, model), group in df.groupby(['Asset Class', 'Model']):
   agg_row = {'Asset Class': aclass, 'Model': model}
   for col in [metric_names[m] for m in metrics]:
       agg_row[col] = weighted_mean(group, col)
   agg_rows.append(agg_row)
agg = pd.DataFrame(agg_rows).round(4)
def style_best_values(tbl):
   style_df = pd.DataFrame('', index=tbl.index, columns=tbl.columns)
   for col in tbl.columns:
       if col in higher_is_better:
           best = tbl[col].idxmax()
       elif col == bias_col:
           best = (tbl[col].abs()).idxmin()
       else:
           best = tbl[col].idxmin()
       style_df.loc[best, col] = (
           f'color: {amundi_dark_blue}; font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.08em; text-decoration: underline'
       )
   return style_df

# ---- DISPLAY ----

"""))

       f"margin-bottom:5px; margin-top:-10px'>{full_name}</div>"
   ))
   styler = tbl.style \
       .format({
           "Mean Absolute Error": "{:.3f}",

           "R² (Explained Variance)": "{:.3f}",

       }) \
       .set_table_styles(styles) \
       .apply(style_best_values, axis=None) \
       .applymap(lambda _: f'background-color: {soft_gray}', subset=pd.IndexSlice[tbl.index[1::2], :])
   display(styler)

Model Performance Summary¶

This table presents the aggregated performance metrics for all tested models—including ARIMA, Random Forest, XGBoost, and three distillate models (Distillate RF, Distillate XGB, Distillate Ensemble)—for cash liquidity forecasting at T+1 across all asset classes.

Key Insights by Asset Class¶

Equity Portfolios

  • Both Random Forest and XGBoost achieve very low prediction errors and high R² scores, outperforming the ARIMA baseline by a large margin.
  • The Distillate RF model attains metrics nearly identical to the parent Random Forest model, but this likely reflects overfitting, as evidenced by its exceptionally low errors and the fact that it exactly matches the RF on test performance. This is a common issue when using top features selected from the same RF for distillation, especially in settings with limited test data.
  • Distillate Ensemble perform competitively. Fixed Income Portfolios
  • Here, Random Forest outperforms XGBoost, and the distillate models (especially XGB and Ensemble) show only a minor loss in accuracy relative to the parent models.
  • All ML models outperform ARIMA by a substantial margin, underlining the value of feature-driven machine learning in fixed income liquidity forecasting. Multi Asset Portfolios
  • The overall pattern is similar to fixed income: XGBoost and its distillates achieve strong results, and all ML models are superior to ARIMA.
  • The performance gap between full and distillate models remains small, indicating that most of the predictive power is concentrated in the top features.

Overall Conclusions¶

  • **Distillate models* can achieve accuracy close to their parent models with many fewer features, supporting their use for interpretability and practical deployment.
  • Distillate RF for equity portfolios shows likely signs of overfitting, as it exactly matches the parent RF, which may not be sustainable out-of-sample.
  • ARIMA is consistently outperformed by ML models across all asset classes, confirming that more sophisticated approaches are needed for modern liquidity management.

VI. Conclusion¶

This report presented a comprehensive comparison of time series regression models for cash liquidity forecasting, including ARIMA, Random Forest, XGBoost, and three distillation models (distilled Random Forest, distilled XGBoost, and a feature-ensemble distillate). Models were evaluated per asset class (Equity, Fixed Income, Multi-Asset) using PV-weighted metrics for robust, actionable insights.

Model Performance:

  • The XGBoost model consistently delivered the highest out-of-sample performance (in RMSE and R²), especially for Fixed Income portfolios.
  • For Equity and Multi-Asset classes, Random Forest and XGBoost both performed well, while ARIMA lagged due to non-stationarity and lack of exogenous features.

Distillation Models:

  • The distilled Random Forest occasionally matched or beat the parent RF on test data, but its much better training performance is evidence of overfitting.
  • Both the distilled XGBoost and ensemble distillate models achieved nearly the same accuracy as their parent models on the test set, indicating they are strong candidates for interpretability with minimal performance loss.

Feature Importance Analysis:

  • Liquidity-related features (containing “liquidity”) accounted for the biggest part of total model importance across asset classes, making them the dominant predictors.
  • Macroeconomic indicators (“US” or “EU”) contributed were secound what reflecting the effect of external economic signals.
  • The remaining importance came from “other” features, such as technical or fund-specific attributes.

Model Robustness:

  • Differences in key test metrics (e.g., R², MAE) among models were generally small (0.01–0.03), confirming stability of the ML approaches. The exception was the distilled RF, which exhibited higher train–test variance and is likely overfitting.

Business Implications:

  • Advanced ML models—especially XGBoost and feature-ensemble distillates—offer robust, interpretable solutions for liquidity forecasting.
  • Distillation is valuable for model simplification, but requires careful validation to avoid overfitting.
